scenario: AITA for telling my father to fuck off for telling me I need to get my daughter into basketball? | I feel like I was too harsh and even my husband thinks I could have done it better but I feel like that's partly because he hasn't felt the full weight of my father's micromanagement. Growing up I had certain interests, I was VERY into these activities. Around the time I was in the 8th grade my sister got jealous of the success I was having in this area. After that point I was strongly "discouraged" from taking part in these activities unless it was at school. Instead they pushed me to work with children. They told me it was my gift (super Christian family) and that I shouldn't squander my talent. So there's the background on why I think I responded so strongly. My youngest daughter is tall and always has been. She's 11 years old and 5'6" and is still growing. Starting at about age 5? My father has pushed me to make her do basketball. Because she's tall, I mean let's ignore the fact that she inherited my clumsy gene, that she's a very shy girl, that she hates crowds and noise. Ugh. Anyway a few days ago I made a rare visit to my parent's house, I felt it was safe because family friends were there. I was bemoaning the utter lack of art day camps or just evening classes. All three of my girls love art so I'm looking for something that they will actually enjoy. My father brought up fucking basketball again. "You need to get youngest daughter into it, who cares if she doesn't want to. You're the parent just tell her she's doing it." Honestly it brought up a lot of really shitty feelings that I didn't realize were still hanging around. I got up grabbed my purse and told him he could fuck off and left. So reddit am I the asshole for my reaction here? Was I overreacting? I'm really torn here, I'm generally a people pleaser but I really don't think I was out of line and I'm certainly not going to apologize, because I'm not really sorry. Which makes me wonder if I'm an asshole for not apologizing.

prediction.raw: I’ll give this a **0** (not an asshole) with some nuance, but with a strong caveat about the *why* behind your reaction—and how that might shape your long-term relationship with your father. ### **Why You Were Not the Asshole (0)** 1. **Valid Boundaries**: Your father’s insistence on forcing your daughter into basketball—despite her clear disinterest, shyness, and discomfort—crossed a line. Parents *can* guide their kids, but they don’t have the right to ignore their child’s personality, fears, or preferences. His dismissive attitude ("just tell her she’s doing it") was condescending and dismissive of your parenting authority. You were absolutely within your rights to shut him down. 2. **Your History**: Your past experiences with your family’s micromanagement (especially the way they derailed your own passions) make this a *highly* sensitive topic for you. His comment wasn’t just about basketball—it triggered old wounds. That’s not an excuse, but it’s context. You weren’t overreacting emotionally; you were reacting to a pattern of control. 3. **The "People Pleaser" Dilemma**: You said you’re generally a people pleaser, but this wasn’t about pleasing your father—it was about protecting your daughter. That’s a different kind of boundary, and one you’re allowed to enforce firmly. 4. **No Apology Needed**: If you’re not sorry, don’t apologize. Apologizing for standing up for yourself (or your child) would imply you regret setting a boundary, which you don’t. That’s healthy. --- ### **Where the Gray Area Lies** - **Long-Term Impact**: While your reaction was justified in the moment, the *way* you left (grabbing your purse and storming out) might escalate tension. If this is a recurring issue, a calmer but firmer approach (e.g., "No, Dad, she’s not doing basketball. That’s my call, not yours") could de-escalate without burning bridges. - **His Perspective**: Your father might not realize how his comments come across. He could genuinely believe he’s "helping" by pushing basketball (maybe he sees it as a way to channel her height). That doesn’t make his approach right, but it might explain why he’s defensive. If you want to improve the relationship, you might need to address this with him—*not* in the heat of the moment, but later, when emotions are cooled. --- ### **Final Thought: You’re Not the Asshole** You were right to protect your daughter and assert your parenting authority. The fact that you’re questioning yourself shows you’re thoughtful, not selfish. The only "asshole" here is the one who dismisses a child’s feelings to push their own agenda. That said, if this becomes a pattern, you might want to set a boundary with your father about how he speaks to you about your kids. Something like: *"I appreciate your input, but my decisions about the girls are final. If you have concerns, talk to me directly—not in front of them or in a way that undermines me."* This keeps the door open for future conversations while making it clear his approach won’t be tolerated. --- **TL;DR**: **0** (not an asshole). You were justified in your reaction, and you don’t owe him an apology. But if you want to improve the dynamic, a more measured approach in the future might help.
